newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korean strike call meets with weak response.
newsitem.headline: South Korean strike call meets with weak response.

text.p: Sporadic street protests and a lack of taxis were the only indications in Seoul that a strike billed as the biggest in South Korea's history had begun on Tuesday.
Subways, buses and banks were working normally and for the nation's two biggest ports it was business as usual.
Most workers ignored calls by the official Federation of Korean Trade Unions for all-out stoppages, a move analysts said showed the organisation had lost much of its militant drive.
Taxi drivers were the only workers to join with any enthusiasm strike protests against a controversial labour law that allows firms to dismiss workers and replace strikers.
Several thousand white collar workers from banks and brokerages waved colourful balloons and sang songs at a "necktie" rally at lunchtime in Seoul's Pagoda Park.
Many were dressed in black neck-ties "to wish death on the labour law", one broker said.
But the outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions vowed its 500,000 members would heed a call for indefinite stoppages unless the law is scrapped by midnight on Tuesday.
"We will concentrate our entire capacity to enforce the full-out strikes," Kwon Young-kil, president of the militant confederation, told a news conference.
Its members had scheduled a march later in the day on a Seoul cathedral where their leaders are sheltering from arrest.
The federation ordered a two-day stoppage by its 1.2 million members on Tuesday and Wednesday, billed as the biggest in the country's history.

The government threatened to take unspecified legal action against international labour leaders who have descended on Seoul in a show of solidarity for strikers. It said they were intervening in the dispute, local media reported.

John Evans, general secretary of the Trade Union Advisory Committee to the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), said the activities of the overseas labour leaders were not unusual.
"This is completely normal. The abnormality is the attitude of the government," he told Reuters.
Strikes were not even the main story on early network news broadcasts.
They were upstaged by coverage of a former Japanese cabinet minister whose defence of Japan's 1910-45 colonial rule over the Korean peninsula has sparked outrage.
Stock investors took heart from the weak strike response. The composite index had soared 2.84 percent, or 18.71 points, to 678.25 by the midday break.

"Investors now have a sort of immunity to the strikes as they have lasted for a long time. Today the crisis was expected to deepen but the reality was different," said Park Byung-moon, head of sales at LG Securities, told Reuters.
The southeast city of Ulsan, home of the giant Hyundai conglomerate, was largely peaceful.
Hyundai Motors had earlier closed down its car plants, the largest in the country, after a worker go-slow.
However, auto workers have now occupied the plants and on Tuesday held noisy rallies by idle production lines, singing and chanting anti-government slogans and banging drums.
The government argues a more flexible labour market is urgently needed to help companies cut costs and boost their competitiveness while exports are slumping.
The legislation passed on December 26 has sparked wildcat strikes organised mainly by the militant confederation.
Kim Jung-youl, a fellow at Korea University's Labour Education and Research Institute, said the response by federation members highlighted the group's moderate nature.
"All militant unions which used to belong to the federation quit it to form the confederation. A lot of those remaining in the federation are not used to staging strikes," Kim said.
Union leaders said the impact of strikes would be more serious on Wednesday when telecommunications workers and subway and bus drivers belonging to the confederation were due to walk out.
